title: Number System & Simplification
intro: Number System is the quiet workhorse of SSC Quant. Divisibility rules, HCF and LCM, unit-digit cycles and BODMAS simplification appear in almost every paper, and the speed you build here carries into percentages, ratios and the rest of arithmetic. The trick is to stop computing the long way: learn the rules, spot the pattern, and finish in seconds. This chapter takes you from the classification of numbers through surds and indices, with the exact short-cuts SSC rewards.

topics.name: Classification of Numbers
topics.details: Numbers are organised into nested families: natural numbers (1, 2, 3, ...), whole numbers (0 included), integers (negatives too), rational numbers (any p/q with q not 0, including terminating and recurring decimals) and irrational numbers (non-terminating, non-repeating decimals such as root 2 or pi). A prime has exactly two factors; 1 is neither prime nor composite; 2 is the only even prime. Knowing where a number sits — and that there are 25 primes below 100 — answers many SSC one-liners instantly.

solved.problem: How many prime numbers are there between 1 and 50?

solved.solution: A recurring decimal is rational. It equals 27/99 = 3/11, so it is rational.

solved.problem: Find the smallest prime number greater than 90.
solved.solution: 91 = 7 x 13 (not prime), 92 to 96 composite, 97 is prime. Answer 97.

solved.problem: How many composite numbers lie between 10 and 20 (exclusive)?

The only even prime number is?

topics.name: Divisibility Rules
topics.details: Divisibility rules let you test a number without dividing. By 2: last digit even. By 3: digit sum divisible by 3. By 4: last two digits divisible by 4. By 5: ends in 0 or 5. By 6: divisible by 2 and 3. By 8: last three digits divisible by 8. By 9: digit sum divisible by 9. By 11: alternating digit-sum difference is 0 or a multiple of 11. For a missing digit, write the rule as an equation and solve.

solved.solution: Last digit 2 -> divisible by 2. Digit sum 7+3+8+4+9+2 = 33 -> divisible by 3. So yes, divisible by 6.

solved.problem: For what digit x is 47x5 divisible by 9?
solved.solution: Digit sum 4+7+x+5 = 16+x must be a multiple of 9. 16+x = 18 -> x = 2.
Last three digits 040 = 40, and 40/8 = 5. Yes, divisible by 8.
Alternating sum from right: 3-9+5-0+8 = 7, not 0 or a multiple of 11, so not divisible by 11.

unsolved.problem: Find x if 12x4 is divisible by 4.

topics.name: HCF & LCM
topics.details: HCF (greatest common divisor) is the largest number dividing all the given numbers; LCM (least common multiple) is the smallest number all of them divide. Use prime factorisation: HCF takes the lowest powers of common primes, LCM the highest powers of all primes. The identity HCF x LCM = product of the two numbers is a constant SSC favourite. Word problems about bells ringing together, tiles, or the largest measuring rod are LCM/HCF in disguise.

solved.problem: Find the HCF and LCM of 24 and 36.
The HCF of two numbers is 8 and their LCM is 96. If one number is 32, find the other.
solved.solution: Product = HCF x LCM = 8 x 96 = 768. Other = 768/32 = 24.

solved.problem: Find the least number divisible by 12, 15 and 20.
Three bells ring at intervals of 6, 8 and 12 seconds. After how many seconds do they ring together?

unsolved.problem: Two numbers are in ratio 3:4 and their LCM is 84. Find them.
Largest number dividing 70 and 125 leaving remainders 5 and 8?
Least number leaving remainder 3 when divided by 5, 6 and 8?

topics.name: Factors & Unit Digit
topics.details: The number of factors of N = p^a x q^b x r^c is (a+1)(b+1)(c+1). The unit digit of a power follows a cycle of length at most 4: 2 cycles 2,4,8,6; 3 cycles 3,9,7,1; 7 cycles 7,9,3,1. To find the unit digit of a^n, reduce n using the cycle (effectively mod 4) and read the matching digit. Digits 0,1,5,6 always repeat themselves.

solved.solution: 7 cycles 7,9,3,1 (length 4). 53 mod 4 = 1, so unit digit = first in cycle = 7.

solved.problem: How many odd factors does 90 have?
solved.solution: 90 = 2 x 3^2 x 5. Drop the 2: 3^2 x 5 has (2+1)(1+1) = 6 odd factors.

unsolved.problem: How many even factors does 72 have?

topics.name: BODMAS & Simplification
topics.details: Simplification tests order of operations: BODMAS — Brackets, Of/Orders (powers), Division, Multiplication, Addition, Subtraction. Work brackets inside-out, convert 'of' to multiplication, then divide and multiply left to right, finally add and subtract. With fractions, convert mixed numbers to improper fractions first, and cancel common factors before multiplying to keep numbers small.

solved.solution: Division and multiplication left to right: 6/2 = 3, 3 x 3 = 9, then 12 + 9 = 21.

topics.name: Surds & Indices
topics.details: An index (exponent) tells how many times a base multiplies itself; a surd is an irrational root such as root 2. The laws of indices (product, quotient, power-of-power, zero and negative exponents) turn ugly expressions into simple ones. To rationalise a denominator like 1/(root a + root b), multiply top and bottom by the conjugate (root a - root b). Compare surds by raising both to the LCM of their root orders.

solved.problem: Which is larger, cube root of 4 or square root of 3?
solved.solution: Raise both to power 6: (4^(1/3))^6 = 16; (3^(1/2))^6 = 27. So root 3 is larger.

shortcuts: Divisibility by 11: alternate-add the digits; difference 0 or 11 means divisible.
Number of factors: add 1 to each prime exponent and multiply.
Unit digit: reduce the power mod 4 and read the cycle.
HCF x LCM = product of the two numbers — finds a missing number fast.
BODMAS: division and multiplication rank equally — go strictly left to right.
mistakes: Treating 1 as a prime number (it is not).
Doing addition before multiplication in simplification.
Forgetting LCM of fractions = LCM(numerators) / HCF(denominators).
Reading power mod 4 = 0 as the FIRST digit of the cycle instead of the LAST.
pyq: SSC Tier 1 leans on quick divisibility, unit-digit and HCF/LCM word problems; Tier 2 adds layered simplification with fractions and surds. Bells/tiles/measuring-rod problems are LCM/HCF; remainder problems usually reduce to HCF of differences.

summary: Classify numbers, apply divisibility rules, factorise for HCF/LCM (HCF x LCM = product), count factors with (a+1)(b+1)..., find unit digits via the mod-4 cycle, and simplify strictly by BODMAS. These rules convert long arithmetic into one-line answers.
